title: Who answers the distressed
hook: who answers the one in distress when he calls, and removes the evil (27:62)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bilqis, the queen who consulted before she acted. Your line was she thought it through.

The car skids on ice. The doctor walks in with a face that's too careful. In that second, before any thinking, some people who rarely pray hear themselves say please, God. Not a formal prayer. Just a call, with nothing else left to try. Near the end of An-Naml, a run of questions about the signs of God reaches exactly that moment.

The passage goes like a drumbeat. Who created the heavens and the earth, sent down rain and grew gardens with it? Is there a god beside God? Who made the earth a fixed place, ran rivers through it, set the mountains, and put a barrier between the two seas? Is there a god beside God? Then verse sixty-two: who answers the one in distress when he calls on Him, and removes the evil, and makes you successors on the earth? Is there a god beside God? The word for the distressed is al-mudtarr. The classical dictionaries give it the sense of being forced, driven into a corner: not just sad, but with no other options left. The verse doesn't say the righteous, or the one who prays perfectly. It says the cornered one, when he calls. Some commentators link it to another passage, where people in a storm at sea call on God sincerely and then, safe on land, forget. The call itself is heard. That's why the verse sits among the signs, with rain and rivers and mountains: being answered in a corner is offered as something people know from their own lives, as plain as weather. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi names three prayers answered without doubt: of the one who is wronged, of the traveler, and of a parent. Muslim teachers add that being answered doesn't always mean getting exactly what was asked. In their reading, the verse promises that the call is heard.
screen: `IS THERE A GOD BESIDE GOD?` · `RAIN, RIVERS, MOUNTAINS, SEAS.` · `AL-MUDTARR: THE CORNERED ONE.` · `THE CALL IS HEARD.`

segments.voice: Find the worry that sits under everything this week, and name it plainly in your own words, without trying to solve it. If you pray, call on God with it now, in whatever language comes, the way the verse describes. If you don't, say it out loud to the quiet, and set it down for this minute.
Al-mudtarr. The cornered, distressed one, named in An-Naml's question of who answers them when they call and lifts the harm. Today's word.
Your line: he answers the distressed. Even a call from a corner is heard. Go gently.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite 27:62 in times of trouble and call on God in their own words in du'a, believing that the prayer of the one in distress is heard.

original.note: Arabic: the one in distress, from a root meaning forced or compelled.

trapdoor: what you thought: God answers prayers.
what it means: the call of someone with nowhere else to turn is heard, and the verse counts that as a sign, like rain.
what a scholar hears: al-mudtarr, from d-r-r through the form of compulsion; 27:62 sits in the refrain 'a-ilahun ma'a Allah', and commentators tie it to the sailors' sincere call in 29:65.

chat.says: Does God only listen to people who pray all the time?
options: An-Naml says He answers the distressed one who calls, not only the righteous.
Yes. The verse promises answers only to those who pray perfectly.
No, but being answered always means getting exactly what you asked.
chat.meaning: Verse 27:62 asks who answers al-mudtarr, the cornered one, when he calls. It names the one in distress, not the one who prays perfectly.

notes: No direct quotations; 27:59–64 paraphrased. The order of questions (creation and rain; the earth, rivers, mountains, two seas; the distressed) follows 27:60–62; confirm.
Hadith of three answered prayers: Abu Dawud 1536, Tirmidhi 1905 cited from memory; versions differ slightly ('the oppressed' / 'the wronged'); confirm.
Root note: mudtarr from d-r-r (form VIII, idtarra, 'to be compelled'); confirm.
